The elder Wyeth's demanding tutelage shaped his son's discipline and technical mastery. But it was N.C.'s sudden death in 1945—killed when his car stalled on railroad tracks near their home—that many believe transformed Andrew's art, deepening it with the melancholy and mortality that would define his greatest work.

Wyeth divided his life between two places that became his enduring subjects: the rolling hills of the Brandywine Valley in Pennsylvania and the coastal town of Cushing, Maine, where the family spent summers.

Wyeth worked primarily in two demanding, old-fashioned media: watercolor and egg tempera, the latter an ancient technique requiring pigment mixed with egg yolk that produced his characteristically dry, muted, and meticulously detailed surfaces.

His palette was famously restrained—browns, grays, ochres, and the bleached tones of winter fields and weathered wood. He painted the everyday world with almost photographic precision, yet his finest works transcended mere realism, evoking loneliness, isolation, and a quiet sense of the passage of time.

"I paint my life," Wyeth often said, and indeed his art drew almost exclusively from the people, houses, and landscapes immediately around him.

## Iconic Works and Famous Subjects

Wyeth's most famous painting, **"Christina's World" (1948)**, depicts a woman lying in a vast, dry field, gazing toward a distant gray farmhouse. The subject, Christina Olson, was a neighbor in Maine paralyzed by a degenerative muscular condition. The image—at once realistic and deeply enigmatic—became one of the most recognized paintings in American art and entered the collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

The disclosure created a media sensation, raising questions about the nature of the artist's relationship with his model and generating enormous publicity.

Andrew Wyeth leaves behind a body of work that speaks powerfully to the American imagination—images of solitary figures, empty rooms, and windswept fields that seem to capture something essential about rural life and human isolation.
